subject: Degrees of freedom for n/L when k = 1

messages.author: 17b53ceda886e27f
messages.subject: Degrees of freedom for n/L when k = 1
parts:
Dear list,

I ran a line transect analysis with only a single transect (k = 1)
and now I am trying to understand how Distance computes degrees of
freedom in this case.
As far as I understood
1) Since empirical estimation is not possible Distance automatically
assumes a Poisson distribution for n, i.e. var(n) is computed as n
(or overdisp * n if an overdispersion factor has been specified)
2) Since degrees of freedom for the encounter rate are zero (df(n/L)
= 0) confidence intervalls of n/L are based upon quantiles of the
normal distributon instead of the t-distribution.
3) The degrees of freedom of the object or school density (Ds) is set
equal to the degrees of freedom of f(0), i.e. df(Ds) = df[f(0)]

What I can not reconstruct is how Distance computes the degrees of
freedom for the density of individuals (D). In general this is done
by the Satterthwaite approximation described on page 78 in the 2001
Distance book, but this does not work here since df(n/L)=0.

So the question is: Are the three statements above correct an how
does Distance compute df(D) when df(n/L) = 0?

Thanks and best regards

Felix

messages.subject: Re: Degrees of freedom for n/L when k = 1
parts:
Dear Jeff,

thanks for your fast response. Yes, Distance gives a value for df(D)
in this case and confidence intervals seem to be computed as usual by
assuming that D is log-normally distributed (p. 77 Distance book)

Felix
